quote: Ist es möglich, dass die Division durch 0 gilt, wenn
english: Is it possible that division by 0 holds, if
topic: Hilbert notes that most of his mathematical ideas came to him outdoors and remarks on choosing a vocation early, then sketches proofs from the axioms of the existence of 0 and 1 and of 0·b = 0, and begins a question about division by 0.

triage.modern_statement: The fragment is cut off before Hilbert's condition, but the context makes it clear enough. Having derived 0·b = 0 from the field axioms, Hilbert asks whether 0 could also have a multiplicative inverse. In modern terms: in a ring (or field) with 1, can there be an element x with 0·x = 1? Since 0·x = 0, this would force 1 = 0, which gives only the trivial zero ring. So the answer is no unless the structure collapses to {0}, or unless the axioms are changed, as in wheels or meadows.
triage.answered_by: This is a standard elementary consequence of the ring and field axioms; no particular person is credited with it. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Later work that changes the axioms on purpose so that x/0 is defined includes J. Carlström, 'Wheels – On Division by Zero' (Stockholm University report 2001:11).

evidence.claim: The zero ring is the only ring where 0 is a unit, i.e. its own multiplicative inverse. So an inverse for 0 forces the trivial ring.
In the standard number systems, zero has no multiplicative inverse under any circumstances.
Wheels are algebras in the universal-algebra sense in which division is always defined, including division by zero. This requires changing the usual field axioms.
Carlström shows that any ring can be extended to a wheel in a structure-preserving way, so division can be made total.

triage.why: The note sits next to Hilbert's derivations of 0, 1 and 0·b = 0 from the axioms. That suggests a teaching or foundations exercise about the independence and consistency of the field axioms, not an open problem. Under the usual axioms the answer follows in one line: 0·b = 0 means 0 can have an inverse only if 1 = 0. Wheels and similar structures that allow division by zero are a small niche topic, not a continuation of this note. Confidence is medium rather than high because the sentence breaks off before the 'if' condition, so I can't be sure which modified axiom system Hilbert had in mind. No source links this specific note to later work.
